nodes.label: Nancy Christie
nodes.date_label: A Full-Orbed Christianity, with Michael Gauvreau (1996) · Engendering the State (2000) · Christian Churches and Their Peoples, with Michael Gauvreau (2010)
nodes.description: A Canadian historian of family, welfare and religion whose work asks how liberal authority was made through everyday institutions. In her 2009 contribution to the liberal-order debate, Christie credits Ian McKay’s framework with connecting cultural and social research while disputing its periodization, its emphasis on the state and its property-based account of individualism. Drawing on Bruce Curtis’s distinction between liberalism and governmentality, she asks for a more precise account of power. She proposes treating churches, voluntary associations and households as places where liberal values were made and contested, so that women’s participation, not only their exclusion, becomes part of the explanation. Engendering the State (2000) and her books with Michael Gauvreau on Protestant churches and social welfare place these institutions at the centre of Canadian social history.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996), with Michael Gauvreau; Engendering the State: Family, Work, and Welfare in Canada (2000); Christian Churches and Their Peoples, 1840–1965 (2010), with Michael Gauvreau.

nodes.label: J. R. Miller
nodes.date_label: Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989) · Shingwauk’s Vision (1996) · Compact, Contract, Covenant (2009)
nodes.description: A settler historian of Indigenous–newcomer relations, residential schooling and treaties in Canada. Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989) is his history of Indian–white relations in Canada. Shingwauk’s Vision (1996), a cross-Canada history of residential schooling, shifts the focus of responsibility from the churches toward the federal government and, ultimately, Euro-Canadian society. Celia Haig-Brown’s review credits the book’s breadth and research while criticizing how examples drawn across places and decades flatten differences among nations and schools, and questioning its claims to balance and its treatment of resistance. Compact, Contract, Covenant (2009) carries his work into the history of treaty-making.

nodes.label: Bruce G. Trigger
nodes.date_label: The Children of Aataentsic (1976) · Natives and Newcomers (1985) · A History of Archaeological Thought (1989)
nodes.description: A Canadian archaeologist and ethnohistorian of the Wendat (Huron) and of colonial encounters in northeastern North America. The Children of Aataentsic (1976) combines archaeology, history and ethnology to argue that Iroquoian societies had changed substantially in the centuries before European contact, so that the impact of contact cannot be assessed without understanding that earlier change. Natives and Newcomers (1985) reconsiders Canada’s ‘heroic age’ of exploration and colonization in the same way, and A History of Archaeological Thought (1989) is his history of his own discipline. He wrote the foreword to Georges E. Sioui’s For an Amerindian Autohistory (1992). Emma LaRocque criticizes that foreword as an example of containment, and argues that the cross-cultural approach to which Trigger belonged, though an improvement on earlier racist scholarship, could still distance and Other its subjects.

nodes.label: Caroline Walker Bynum
nodes.date_label: Jesus as Mother: essay collection (1982) · Holy Feast and Holy Fast (1987) · Fragmentation and Redemption (1991)
nodes.description: A historian of medieval European religion, gender and the body. Holy Feast and Holy Fast (1987) argues that food lay at the heart of much late-medieval women’s piety: women renounced ordinary food through fasting to prepare for the extraordinary food of the eucharist, and offered themselves as food in miracles of feeding. Where earlier scholars had treated fasting, stigmata and inedia in isolation or through modern medical and psychological theories, she showed how these practices enabled women to exert control within the family and religious life. In ‘Why All the Fuss about the Body?’ (1995) she engages sympathetically with Judith Butler’s performative account of gender, but insists that medieval and modern ideas of body and identity be compared in their own settings; the Middle Ages, she writes, was characterized by ‘a cacophony of discourses’. Jesus as Mother (1982) and Fragmentation and Redemption (1991) are her other major collections on gender and the body in medieval religion.

nodes.label: Barbara H. Rosenwein
nodes.date_label: Negotiating Space (1999) · “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002) · Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006)
nodes.description: A medieval historian whose studies of property, immunity and power led to an influential approach to the history of emotions. ‘Worrying about Emotions in History’ (2002) revisits Lucien Febvre’s call for a history of feeling and rejects the grand narrative, associated with Norbert Elias, of a movement from unrestrained medieval emotion to modern self-control. In its place she proposes emotional communities: overlapping groups that value and express emotions in different ways. In a 2010 interview she questions William Reddy’s sharp distinction between emotional regimes and emotional refuges; Reddy’s reply allowing plural regimes stands beside her objection. Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006) is the book-length study.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Negotiating Space (1999); “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002); Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006; paperback 2007 distinct); answers in Jan Plamper’s interview (2010).

nodes.label: Joanna Bourke
nodes.date_label: Dismembering the Male (1996) · An Intimate History of Killing (1999) · Fear: A Cultural History (2005)
nodes.description: A historian of modern Britain, war, the body and emotion. Dismembering the Male (1996) studies men’s bodies and masculinity in the First World War. An Intimate History of Killing (1999), drawing on letters, diaries and memoirs of British, American and Australian combatants in the two world wars and Vietnam, argues that the structure of war encouraged pleasure in killing and that ordinary men could become enthusiastic killers without being brutalized. Her later work on fear and pain asks what emotions do: expressions of fear follow learned conventions yet can change the feeling they name, a point she develops through William Reddy’s concept of the emotive.

nodes.label: Keith Thomas
nodes.date_label: “History and Anthropology” (1963) · Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) · Man and the Natural World (1983)
nodes.description: A historian of early modern English beliefs, social relations and attitudes. Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) asks why beliefs in magic, astrology and witchcraft made sense in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century England and why they declined; the inquiry began, he recalls, from a puzzle about astrology and led him to anthropology. His 1963 essay ‘History and Anthropology’ grew from a review of Evans-Pritchard that Lawrence Stone encouraged him to expand. Thomas names Christopher Hill and R. H. Tawney as formative influences, and was drawn to Lucien Febvre’s inquiry into people’s assumptions rather than to quantitative Annales history. He later called his work a descriptive ethnography of early modern England and conceded that his explanation of magic’s decline was incomplete. Jan Machielsen and Michelle Pfeffer’s 2023 reassessment, building on Hildred Geertz’s criticism, questions the book’s categories of religion and magic. Man and the Natural World (1983) traced changing English attitudes to nature.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “History and Anthropology” (1963); Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971); Man and the Natural World (1983); The Ends of Life (2009).
nodes.scope_note: Macfarlane interview timestamps and Machielsen/Pfeffer reassessment verified 2026-10-31. Stone edge rests on the atlas’s earlier accepted reading. Books not read in full.

nodes.label: J. H. Elliott
nodes.date_label: Imperial Spain, 1469–1716 (1963) · “A Europe of Composite Monarchies” (1992) · Empires of the Atlantic World (2006)
nodes.description: A historian of early modern Spain and its empire. His first two books, The Revolt of the Catalans and Imperial Spain, 1469–1716, both appeared in 1963; a biography of the Count-Duke of Olivares followed in 1986. His interest in state formation and ‘composite monarchies’ runs from the Catalan revolt to Scots and Catalans (2018), and Empires of the Atlantic World (2006) compares British and Spanish America. Richard Kagan and Geoffrey Parker’s memoir records his admiration for Lucien Febvre’s regional synthesis and his doubts about how Fernand Braudel joined structures to events; the wish to disprove Braudel, with a belief in political biography, drove the Olivares project. His 1980 review of Carlo Ginzburg questioned how far a single case could represent a wider society. Ginzburg rejected Elliott’s opposition of micro- to macrohistory, and Natalie Zemon Davis rejected a zero-sum choice between histories of Martin Guerre and Martin Luther.

nodes.label: John M. MacKenzie
nodes.date_label: Propaganda and Empire (1984) · Imperialism and Popular Culture: edited collection (1986) · The Empire of Nature (1988)
nodes.description: A historian of empire who made its cultural presence in Britain, and its environmental history overseas, central subjects of imperial history. As founding editor of Manchester University Press’s Studies in Imperialism series he set out to examine how imperialism shaped the dominant societies as well as those they ruled; Propaganda and Empire (1984) studied the manipulation of British public opinion. The Empire of Nature (1988) connected hunting and conservation with British rule in Africa and India. Orientalism: History, Theory and the Arts (1995) challenged Edward Said’s generalizations through empirical study of the arts, as Berny Sèbe describes; Said in turn criticized an approach he associated with MacKenzie that treated culture as propaganda. His exchanges with Bernard Porter, after Porter’s The Absent-Minded Imperialists (2004), became among the most-read items in the Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History.

nodes.label: Callum G. Brown
nodes.date_label: Religion and Society in Scotland since 1707: listed edition 2 (1997) · The Death of Christian Britain: first edition (2001) · Postmodernism for Historians (2005) · Religion and Society in Twentieth-Century Britain (2006)
nodes.description: A social and cultural historian of religion, secularisation and unbelief. Brown’s work moved from class-based measurements of church participation toward the gendered and discursive conditions of Christian identity, with a sharp rupture proposed for the 1960s. That account remains contested. Jeremy Morris accepts criticism of inevitable modernization-to-decline stories while arguing that Brown and others narrow religion too far: institutional decline can coexist with persistent religious identity. Brown’s later “The Necessity of Atheism” approaches the problem from another direction. Using Charles Taylor as a critical foil, he argues that measuring secularity only through religious categories marginalizes lives lived without a god and that medieval disbelief should not be ruled out in advance. The intervention challenges both the assumed religious past and the categories used to describe the secular present; it does not establish a single universal measure of unbelief.
